title: Finnish sauna culture: about three million saunas, the 2020 UNESCO intangible heritage listing, old smoke saunas and a long-term health study

sources.title: UNESCO puts Finnish sauna culture on heritage list (2020-12-17)
Letting off steam: everything you need to know about Finnish sauna
sources.note: 只取事實（文中「可追溯到西元前 7000 年」屬流行說法，不採用）

sources.title: Laukkanen T, et al. Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events (2015)

facts.text: On December 17, 2020, UNESCO added sauna culture in Finland to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.
Finland has about three million saunas for about 5.5 million people.
Most Finns own at least one sauna, and almost 90 percent of Finns take a sauna at least once a week.
The earliest Finnish saunas were smoke saunas dug into hillsides: stones were heated over a wood fire, smoke filled the room, and it was let out before people went in.
Once saunas became separate buildings with ventilation, Finns used them for many tasks, such as heating and preserving food.
Until the 1940s, women in the Finnish countryside often gave birth in saunas.
When Finns settled in a new place, they often built the sauna before the house.
Water thrown on the hot stones of the stove makes steam, which Finns call löyly.
Modern saunas are heated either by wood or by electricity.
Bathers sometimes gently beat their skin with a bundle of birch twigs called a vihta.
A Finnish sauna is usually around 80 degrees Celsius; public saunas at swimming pools are often about 85 degrees.
Between rounds in the heat, especially in winter, Finns cool off in a hole cut in a frozen lake or by rolling in the snow.
In a Finnish sauna people are usually naked, which is seen as putting everyone on the same level; the room is kept quiet, without music.
Finns use the sauna to relax and to socialize, and sometimes even to do business.
During the Cold War, Finnish president Urho Kekkonen practiced sauna diplomacy with Soviet leaders.
Finland held a sauna endurance world championship for 11 years but stopped it in 2010 after a competitor died in a sauna heated to 110 degrees.
A Finnish study followed 2,315 men aged 42 to 60 from eastern Finland for a median of about 20.7 years.
In that study, men who took a sauna 4 to 7 times a week were about half as likely to die of heart and blood vessel disease as men who went once a week.
facts.note: fatal CVD 校正後 HR 0.50（95% CI 0.33–0.77）

facts.text: The same men had about a 40 percent lower risk of death from any cause than once-a-week bathers.
The study was observational: it showed a link but could not prove that the sauna itself caused the lower risk, and the authors called for further trials.
